summary: Baker Range, Delaware River near Port Penn: a 110-foot iron rear tower moved from Reedy Island in 1904, keepers who lived in the marsh, and a front light lost by 1929.

light.note: Temporary headlight lanterns on posts first lit 11 November 1902; permanent front light replaced them 16 September 1904 (LighthouseFriends). Front light focal plane 25 ft (7.6 m) above mean low water. The rear light's focal height is not given in the sources read.

structures.note: Built at Reedy Island Old Rear Range (established 1896), discontinued 16 May 1904, and moved here (LighthouseFriends). The 110 ft figure is the tower height. In 2016 the light moved to a new structure about 3,700 ft south. The historic tower's present state is not described in the sources read.

structures.type: two-story square frame dwelling on piles, hipped roof
structures.note: Front light stood on piles in the marsh; by 1929 only concrete-filled iron pilings remained (LighthouseFriends).

structures.type: steel skeleton tower with white slatted daymark
structures.note: Placed near the southern tip of Reedy Island, 1.9 miles south of the rear tower, when the lights were automated, around 1925 (LighthouseFriends).

staffing.note: Keeper turnover ended around 1925 when the lights were automated (LighthouseFriends).

access.note: Owned by the Coast Guard; tower closed. Visible from Highway 9 north of Port Penn; walking trails give river access (LighthouseFriends).

events.note: Rear tower built for the Reedy Island Old Rear Range (LighthouseFriends)
Lighthouse Board report records the Army Corps channel plan that needed three range sets, Baker among them
Temporary headlight lanterns on posts, 11 November 1902
Permanent front light replaced the temporary light, 16 September 1904
Rear tower moved from Reedy Island Old Rear Range, discontinued 16 May 1904
Keeper William Harrington died in March 1917 (the Saturday before 26 March). Found dying in a wheat field by his wife; died before reaching the house
28 December 1917: Keeper Hill aided two men in an open boat, nearly frozen
26 September 1923: Keeper Hill rescued L. Bartram, stuck in marsh mud
Keeper turnover ended around 1925; rear light lowering mechanism removed
Front station and 7.85 acres offered to the highest bidder; bids to be opened 20 November 1929 (LighthouseFriends, citing the Wilmington Evening Journal of 12 October 1929)
Rear light moved from the historic tower to a new structure about 3,700 ft south

keepers.name: Freddie C. Hill
keepers.note: Also Fred C. Hill (LighthouseFriends, 1917 to 1925, about eight years before automation; Wikipedia 1917 to 1924 not cited). Named in the 1919 Commissioner's report as keeper of Baker Range Light Station. Rescues 1917 and 1923.

keepers.name: Hannah Hill
keepers.note: Wife of Freddie C. Hill; unofficial helper, not on the archive roster. When he was ill she tended the light, per her 1950 congressional testimony as LighthouseFriends quotes it.

corrections.proposed: frame two-story dwelling on piles, built 1904, lost
corrections.why: LighthouseFriends describes the 1904 front light as a square frame dwelling on piles, and says it was replaced on 16 September 1904. No steel 1902 front tower is described. The active steel front light at Reedy Island, from about 1925, is missing from the record.

corrections.proposed: iron, built 1896 at Reedy Island and moved here in 1904, 33.5 m (110 ft), standing
corrections.why: LighthouseFriends describes one rear tower: a 110-foot iron skeleton tower built at Reedy Island in 1896 and moved to Baker in 1904. The 2016 move put the rear light on a new structure about 3,700 ft south, so the historic tower is not the active light, but it is described as standing.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record and the archive give 1902 for the first light. LighthouseFriends confirms temporary lights from 11 November 1902, with permanent front lights from 16 September 1904.

The archive's place record gives the station as established 1902. LighthouseFriends dates the rear tower to 1896 at Reedy Island and its move to Baker to 1904. The 1902 date is the Baker Range station, the 1896 date is the tower.
LighthouseFriends gives 1917 to 1925; the archive's roster gives 1917 to 1926. The end date is not resolved.

resolved_conflicts.field: distance between front and rear lights
resolved_conflicts.explanation: LighthouseFriends gives 760 yards (about 695 m) between the front and rear lights in one passage and roughly 2,000 feet (about 610 m) in another. The story states both.

notes_for_editor: Sources: LighthouseFriends (facts and its own quotations: the 1900 report on the channel, the 1906 report on the tower, Hill's 1917 letter and Hannah Hill's 1950 testimony, as LighthouseFriends prints them; the 1900 passage is not located in the corpus, which has no page index for that volume, so the story attributes it to LighthouseFriends' quotation); the USLHS roster by slug; the Evening Journal of 26 March 1917, p. 12 (checked on the page: 'Saturday night' before a Monday paper is 24 March 1917; the OCR reads 'In 111 health' and 'Add' for 'field'); Lighthouse Service Bulletin 1918 PDF p. 12 (checked, OCR: F. C. Hill's 28 December 1917 rescue); Bulletin 1923 PDF p. 55 (checked, OCR interleaved: 'F. C. Hill, keeper of Baker Range Rear Light Station' rescued a man on September 26); Commissioner's report volume, scan p. 460 printed p. 60 (checked, 1919 keepers list). Not used: Wikipedia leads (first lit 1904, Fred C. Hill 1917 to 1924). The Smyrna Times of 28 March 1917 reads 'William Barrington, aged 62' in OCR, not used. The archive lists Mary Harrington for 1917 without a link to the widow in any source. The 1929 Evening Journal notice was not found in Chronicling America's Delaware 1923-1935 search, so it is cited to LighthouseFriends. LighthouseFriends says the keeper's dwelling and foundation blocks 'remain standing at the tower's former site in Port Penn', and it places the former rear-light site at the north end of Congress Street; the story says nothing about these because the sources do not say which structure stands where now. The focal-height correction was dropped: the 33.5 m in the record is the tower height, and the only focal plane in the sources is the front light's, 25 ft (7.6 m) above mean low water. Hannah Hill is named from LighthouseFriends' quotation of her 1950 testimony, not checked at source.
